functional.text: Upload and download files of any size (up to 50 GB) from any device.
Sync: a change on one device appears automatically on the user's other devices and for collaborators on shared folders.
Version history: restore any version (including deleted files) from the last 30 days.
Share folders with other users (view or edit).
Offline edits are queued and synced when the device reconnects.

non_functional.text: Durability: an acknowledged file is never lost (11 nines).
Sync latency: changes visible on other online devices within ~10 s.
Bandwidth efficient and resumable: only changed chunks are transferred; uploads resume after a dropped connection.
No silent overwrites: all devices converge to the same tree; concurrent edits are kept.
Metadata available 99.9%+; uploads may degrade gracefully.

assumptions.text: 500M users, 100M DAU, ~2 devices online per DAU, ~10 file changes per DAU per day, ~1 MB per change on average.
~5 GB stored per user on average; ~1,000 files per user.

out_of_scope.text: Real-time co-editing inside a document, full-text search of file contents, billing.

api.notes: Only missing chunks are uploaded; URLs expire in ~15 min.
Goes to the storage edge, not our servers; idempotent because the key is the hash.
Atomic: the version exists only once every chunk is in the block store.
Delta since the cursor (namespace seqs); the same call after a long offline period.
Long-poll; returns early when a namespace changes.

data.name: file_journal
data.fields: namespace_id, seq (PK per namespace), path, rev, block_hashes[], size, deleted, device_id, ts
data.why: Append-only per namespace: current tree, version history and sync cursor in one table; sharded by namespace_id.

data.name: block_index
data.fields: hash (PK, SHA-256), size, ref_count, location, created_at
data.why: Answers 'which chunks are missing' and drives chunk garbage collection; sharded by hash.

data.name: namespaces
data.fields: namespace_id, owner_id, members[(user_id, role)], mount_path per member
data.why: Shared folders are namespaces mounted into several users' trees.

data.name: chunks
data.why: Immutable, content-addressed objects; dedup is free.

parts.title: Chunked, resumable upload with dedup
parts.problem: Move ~1B file changes a day (~12 GB/s in) from flaky laptops and phones, files up to 50 GB, without re-sending unchanged bytes or restarting from zero after a drop.

options.name: whole file through the app servers
options.cons: 50 GB uploads pin app servers; a drop restarts from zero; a 1-byte edit re-sends the whole file

options.name: whole file straight to object storage via a presigned URL
options.pros: app servers stay out of the byte path
options.cons: still all-or-nothing per file; no dedup; every edit re-uploads everything

options.name: content-addressed 4 MB chunks: client hashes, server answers which are missing, client PUTs only those via presigned URLs
options.pros: dedup across versions (and users); resume per chunk; parallel uploads; app servers only see hashes
options.cons: a block index to maintain; smarter client; cross-user dedup can leak that a file exists

parts.choice: 4 MB content-addressed chunks (SHA-256), uploaded directly to the storage edge with presigned URLs; only missing hashes are sent
parts.why: Most edits touch a few chunks of a file, so the chunk diff cuts the ~12 GB/s ingress sharply and dedup saves a large share of 2.5 EB. A dropped connection loses at most one 4 MB chunk. App servers only handle metadata, so they scale with commits (~35k/s peak), not bytes.

nodes.label: Desktop / mobile client (watcher, chunker, local DB)
Block store: 4 MB chunks by SHA-256
Metadata DB (sharded by namespace): journal, versions, block index

parts.title: Metadata and version history
parts.problem: Store the file tree, every version for 30 days and shared folders (~500B file rows, ~500 TB) so that commits are atomic and each device can ask 'what changed since I last looked?'.

options.name: one SQL database with a files table
options.cons: 500 TB and ~35k commits/s at peak don't fit one primary

options.name: NoSQL document per file
options.cons: no transactions across files (folder moves); no natural ordered change log per folder

options.name: SQL sharded by namespace (a user's root or a shared folder) with an append-only journal per namespace
options.pros: transactions inside a namespace; the journal's seq is both version history and the sync cursor
options.cons: huge shared folders become hot shards; moves across namespaces need two steps

parts.choice: SQL sharded by namespace_id, with an append-only journal (namespace_id, seq) per namespace
parts.why: Almost every operation stays inside one namespace, so a shard can give it a transaction and a strictly increasing seq. One table then answers three questions: current tree (latest row per path), history (all rows per path, 30 days), and sync (rows with seq > cursor).

nodes.label: Metadata DB (sharded by namespace): journal, versions, block index

parts.title: Sync: telling other devices about changes
parts.problem: About 200M devices are online at a time. Each must learn within ~10 s that something changed in one of its namespaces, and catch up after hours offline.

options.name: every device polls /changes every 30 s
options.cons: 200M / 30 s ≈ 6.7M requests/s, almost all empty; up to 30 s delay

options.name: push full change payloads over WebSockets
options.cons: servers hold per-device state and payloads; a reconnect still needs a replay path

options.name: long-poll 'namespace changed' signal, then pull the delta by cursor
options.pros: idle connections are cheap; one catch-up path for online and offline devices
options.cons: ~2,000 servers just to hold connections; one extra round trip per change

parts.choice: Long-poll notification service fed by namespace change events; devices then pull /changes?cursor=
parts.why: The signal is tiny and the data path is the same cursor-based delta that offline devices use (F5), so there is only one way to sync. 200M held connections at ~100k each is ~2,000 notify servers, cheap next to 6.7M polls/s.

nodes.label: Desktop / mobile client (watcher, chunker, local DB)
Metadata DB (sharded by namespace): journal, versions, block index

parts.title: Conflicts between devices
parts.problem: Two devices (or a laptop that was offline for a day) edit the same file from the same base. Neither edit may be lost silently, and all devices must end up with the same tree.

options.name: pessimistic locks (check-out)
options.cons: breaks offline editing; locks get stuck on dead laptops

options.name: optimistic commit on base revision; the loser becomes a 'conflicted copy'
options.cons: users occasionally see a duplicate file to reconcile

options.name: automatic content merge (3-way / OT)
options.cons: most files are binary; wrong merges corrupt files

parts.choice: Optimistic concurrency: commit carries base_rev; on mismatch the server rejects and the client saves its version as 'name (conflicted copy, device, date)'
parts.why: N4 forbids silent loss and F5 requires offline edits, which rules out locks and LWW. Conflicts are rare (few files are edited on two devices at once), so a visible duplicate is an acceptable cost.

nodes.label: Desktop / mobile client (watcher, chunker, local DB)
Metadata DB (sharded by namespace): journal, versions, block index

deep_dives.title: Chunk size and boundaries

options.name: fixed-size 4 MB chunks
options.pros: simple; cheap to hash on phones
options.cons: inserting a byte early in a big file shifts every later chunk boundary

options.name: content-defined chunking (rolling hash, ~4 MB average)
options.pros: boundaries survive inserts, so more dedup on large edited files
options.cons: more CPU on the client; variable chunk sizes complicate the index

deep_dives.choice: Fixed 4 MB chunks by default; content-defined chunking only for large files of formats edited in place
deep_dives.why: The average change is ~1 MB, i.e. one chunk, so fixed chunks lose little. CDC pays off for big files where bytes are inserted in the middle, so it is worth it only there.

deep_dives.title: Garbage-collecting unreferenced chunks

options.name: reference counting on every commit and expiry
options.cons: counts drift under retries and partial failures; one wrong decrement deletes live data

options.name: periodic mark-and-sweep over the journal, with a grace period
options.pros: self-correcting; a bug delays deletion instead of losing data
options.cons: storage is freed days later; a heavy batch job

deep_dives.choice: Mark-and-sweep after the 30-day history window, deleting only chunks unreferenced for 7 more days
deep_dives.why: N1 makes deleting a live chunk the worst possible bug; paying a few days of extra storage is far cheaper than losing a file.

wrapup.bottlenecks: Hot shared namespaces (a company-wide folder) concentrate commits on one metadata shard: split big namespaces or rate-limit; notification fan-out for namespaces with thousands of members; block index lookups during bulk first uploads.
wrapup.failures: Upload dropped: resume from the first missing chunk. Metadata shard primary dies: failover to a sync replica, commits pause seconds. Notify server dies: clients reconnect and pull /changes by cursor, nothing is lost. Block store region issue: erasure coding plus cross-region copies.
wrapup.monitoring: Commit p99 and 409 conflict rate, time from commit to other-device sync (end-to-end probe), chunk upload error/resume rate, dedup ratio, notify connection count, journal lag, GC deleted bytes vs. expected.
wrapup.scale: Add metadata shards by namespace range, more notify servers for connections, and block storage capacity; the byte path scales with the object store, not our servers.
wrapup.future: LAN sync between devices on the same network, selective sync / on-demand files, content search, delta compression inside chunks.
